svg.text: Database Design Fundamentals
Normalization · Primary Keys · Data Types · Constraints · N+1 Problem
Normalization — Eliminate Redundancy
1NF: Atomic Values
❌ users: phones = "081,082"
✅ user_phones: (user_id, phone) — separate table for multi-values
Rule: one value per cell — no arrays, no comma-separated lists
2NF: No Partial Dependencies
❌ order_items: (order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name)
✅ order_items: (order_id, product_id, quantity) · products: (id, name)
Rule: non-key columns depend on the WHOLE composite key
3NF: No Transitive Dependencies
❌ employees: (id, name, dept_id, dept_name, dept_budget)
✅ employees: (id, name, dept_id) · departments: (id, name, budget)
Rule: non-key columns depend on primary key, not other non-key columns
When to Denormalize (intentionally break rules)
✓ Read:Write ratio > 10:1 ✓ JOIN query measured as too slow
✓ READ MODEL in CQRS (already separate from write model)
Rule: normalize first, denormalize ONLY after measuring
Primary Key Strategies
BIGINT (auto-increment)
8 bytes · Sequential writes (good for B-tree) · Predictable (security risk)
✓ Single database ✗ Doesn't work across shards
Use when: small scale, internal IDs not exposed to users
UUID v4 (random)
16 bytes · Globally unique · Unpredictable (secure)
✓ Distributed safe ✗ Random writes break B-tree locality → fragmentation
Use when: distributed systems, user-facing IDs
UUID v7 / ULID — RECOMMENDED ★
16 bytes · Globally unique · TIME-ORDERED (first 48 bits = timestamp)
✓ Globally unique ✓ Sequential writes (no B-tree fragmentation)
Best of both worlds — use for all new distributed systems
Real Company Choices
Twitter/Discord: Snowflake ID (64-bit, time+worker+seq = sortable + unique)
Instagram: custom ID (timestamp+shard+sequence)
Stripe: "ch_", "cus_" prefixed string IDs (readable type prefix + random)
Critical Data Type Rules
✅ DECIMAL(19,4) or store cents as INT (price_cents = 990 = $9.90)
❌ INT for user_id (max 2.1B users) · DATETIME without timezone
✅ BIGINT for IDs · TIMESTAMPTZ (with timezone) for timestamps
❌ VARCHAR(255) for everything (lazy)
✅ Choose appropriate length: CHAR(2) for country, VARCHAR(100) for names
N+1 Query Problem
❌ SELECT * FROM orders (100 rows) + for each order: SELECT user WHERE id=?
= 101 queries! Gets worse as table grows
✅ SELECT o.*, u.name FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id
= 1 query. Always join, or use IN clause for batch fetch
Most ORM "lazy loading" is N+1 by default — always use eager loading
Most common bug that kills app performance at scale
